chapters.1: As David grows old and frail, his son Adonijah tries to seize the throne by declaring himself king with support from Joab and the priest Abiathar. Bathsheba and the prophet Nathan intervene, reminding David of his promise that Solomon would be king, and David quickly has Solomon anointed and proclaimed king instead.
chapters.2: On his deathbed, David instructs Solomon to be strong, follow God's law, and deal firmly with people who had wronged him, including Joab and Shimei. After David dies, Solomon consolidates his power by executing Adonijah, Joab, and others seen as threats, securing his hold on the throne.
chapters.3: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and, after offering sacrifices at Gibeon, has a dream in which God offers to give him anything he asks for; Solomon requests wisdom to govern well rather than wealth or long life, and God grants it along with riches and honor. Solomon's wisdom is immediately demonstrated when he cleverly resolves a dispute between two women over a baby.
chapters.4: This chapter lists Solomon's chief officials and the twelve district governors responsible for supplying the royal household, reflecting the organization of his kingdom. It also summarizes Solomon's extraordinary wisdom and the extent of Israel's prosperity and peace under his reign.
chapters.5: Solomon makes an agreement with King Hiram of Tyre to supply cedar and cypress timber and skilled labor for building the temple in exchange for food provisions. The chapter describes the large workforce of laborers and stonecutters Solomon organizes to prepare materials for the temple's construction.
chapters.6: Solomon builds the temple in Jerusalem according to detailed specifications, including its dimensions, inner sanctuary, cedar paneling, and gold overlay, along with carved cherubim guarding the most holy place. The project takes seven years, and God reaffirms his promise to dwell among Israel if Solomon remains obedient.
chapters.7: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own more elaborate palace complex, and the chapter describes the skilled craftsman Hiram's bronze work for the temple, including two large pillars, an enormous basin called the "sea," and various furnishings. It closes by noting that all the gold and bronze items for temple worship were finally completed and brought in.
chapters.8: Solomon oversees the ark of the covenant being brought into the newly built temple, and God's presence fills the space as a cloud. Solomon offers a long public prayer dedicating the temple, asking God to hear Israel's prayers toward this place, followed by sacrifices and a great national celebration.
chapters.9: God appears to Solomon again, promising to bless his reign if he remains faithful but warning that disobedience will lead to the nation's downfall and the temple's destruction. The chapter also covers Solomon's building projects, labor practices, and his fleet of ships that brought in great wealth.
chapters.10: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon to test his legendary wisdom with difficult questions, and she leaves deeply impressed by his wisdom and the splendor of his kingdom. The chapter also details Solomon's immense wealth, including gold, ivory, and exotic goods from trade.
chapters.11: In his old age, Solomon's many foreign wives lead him into idolatry, worshiping gods like Ashtoreth and Molech, which angers God and leads to a decree that the kingdom will be split after his death. Adversaries like Jeroboam begin to rise, and God tells Jeroboam that he will rule over ten of Israel's tribes.
chapters.12: After Solomon's death, his son Rehoboam refuses to ease the people's heavy labor burdens, prompting ten northern tribes to reject his rule and make Jeroboam their king, splitting the kingdom into Israel (north) and Judah (south). Jeroboam sets up alternative worship centers with golden calves at Bethel and Dan, leading Israel into idolatry.
chapters.13: A prophet confronts Jeroboam at his altar in Bethel, predicting its eventual destruction and performing a miraculous sign, though Jeroboam's hand is temporarily paralyzed and then healed. On his way home, this prophet disobeys God's instructions by eating with another prophet who deceived him, and he is killed by a lion as a consequence.
chapters.14: Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah to ask about their sick son, but Ahijah recognizes her and delivers a harsh prophecy that the child will die and Jeroboam's dynasty will be destroyed for leading Israel into idolatry. The chapter also briefly covers the reign of Rehoboam in Judah, including conflict with Jeroboam and Egyptian plundering of the temple.
chapters.15: This chapter traces the reigns of several kings: Abijam and then Asa in Judah, with Asa noted for removing idols and remaining loyal to God for most of his reign, and Nadab and then Baasha in Israel, with Baasha wiping out Jeroboam's entire family as previously prophesied. The chapter highlights ongoing warfare between Judah and Israel during this period.
chapters.16: This chapter rapidly covers several unstable Israelite kings: Baasha's dynasty is wiped out by Zimri, who himself is killed within days by Omri, who becomes king and builds the city of Samaria. The chapter ends by introducing Ahab, Omri's son, who marries Jezebel and leads Israel into its worst idolatry yet by worshiping Baal.
chapters.17: God sends the prophet Elijah to announce a drought as judgment on Ahab's Israel, and Elijah is miraculously sustained first by ravens at a brook and then by a poor widow in Zarephath whose flour and oil never run out during the famine. Elijah also raises the widow's son from death after he suddenly dies, confirming him as a true prophet of God.
chapters.18: After three years of drought, Elijah confronts King Ahab and challenges the prophets of Baal to a dramatic contest on Mount Carmel to prove whose god is real. When Baal's prophets fail to call down fire despite frantic effort, Elijah's prayer brings fire from heaven to consume his sacrifice, leading the people to execute the false prophets and rain to finally return.
chapters.19: Fleeing Jezebel's death threat after the Mount Carmel victory, an exhausted and discouraged Elijah travels to Mount Horeb, where God speaks to him not through dramatic wind, earthquake, or fire but through a gentle, quiet voice. God reassures Elijah he is not alone, commissions him to anoint new leaders, and directs him to Elisha, who becomes his successor.
chapters.20: Syria's King Ben-hadad besieges Samaria and makes arrogant demands of Ahab, but with a prophet's guidance, Israel's outnumbered forces win two unlikely victories against Syria. Ahab then makes a lenient treaty with the defeated Ben-hadad instead of following God's judgment, and a prophet condemns him for letting a man God had doomed escape.
chapters.21: Ahab covets a vineyard belonging to a man named Naboth, and when Naboth refuses to sell his family inheritance, Queen Jezebel arranges false charges that lead to Naboth's execution so Ahab can seize the land. The prophet Elijah confronts Ahab with God's judgment for this murder, pronouncing disaster on his family line, though Ahab's humble response delays some of the punishment.
chapters.22: King Ahab of Israel persuades Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him in battle against Syria at Ramoth-gilead, ignoring a true but unwelcome prophecy of disaster from Micaiah in favor of false prophets telling him what he wants to hear. Ahab is fatally wounded in the battle despite disguising himself, fulfilling the prophecy, and the chapter closes with brief notes on Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah and the start of Ahaziah's reign in Israel.
